en: Praise of the Madhyamaka Treatise composed by Ācārya Candrakīrti: That ninefold teaching consisting of the sūtras and so forth, which was proclaimed here by the Buddhas—

Skilled in conforming to the conduct of the world and relying upon the two truths, there is no discourse on the destruction of hatred when passion has been eliminated; nor is there any discourse on the destruction of passion when hatred has been eliminated. (1)

Even that teaching which leads to the destruction of pride and the like does not destroy other defilements; therefore, it is not all-pervasive, nor do those various great discourses therein [address them]. But this discourse for the total destruction of delusion [destroys] all afflictions without exception.
For all afflictions have been taught by the Victors to be destroyed when one relies upon delusion. || 2 ||

Since dependent origination and the like have been seen for the sake of the complete destruction of this delusion, that very reality is its remedy; it alone has been proclaimed by the Sugatas as the Middle Way. Furthermore, because the Sage’s body consists of the Dharma, it is called emptiness.
It is proclaimed as the heart of all Buddhas, and it is also known as the Great Vidyā. || 3 ||
Since this [emptiness] has arisen as the source of all qualities, it is therefore described in detail and primarily in its essential nature within the treatise *Madhyamaka* by the Buddhas;
having understood the teaching exactly as it stands, with a mind melted by compassion.
By that wise son of the Buddhas, Nāgārjuna, with reverence. || 4 ||
The teaching of the Jina is profound; indeed, no person understands it, for those who desire to proclaim the reality as something distinct from the words of the Lord of Munis,
and others of evil intellect who explain the scripture otherwise, [do not understand it].
And by refuting those as well, this treatise has been composed, having destroyed the two internal extremes.
It is clear that Nāgārjuna, accompanied by Rāhulabhadra,
lived for a long time with his words followed even by the King;
having defeated all the heretics whose intellects were determined through the discernment of his treatises—
The disciples of Sthūla also maintained the teaching of the eminent Sage for a long time.
When the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, out of compassion, had cut off and given his own head to a beggar who had arrived seeking it, and had departed for Sukhāvatī,
the treatises he composed and his circle of disciples likewise met with destruction after a long period of time.
Now that the sun of reality has set, that doctrine is no longer clearly evident anywhere.
Nowadays, in this world, the Buddhist school has mostly strayed far from the true path; it is preoccupied with mere fanciful imaginings, intoxicated by the wine of logic,
and agitated, lacking the realization of the reality taught by the Omniscient One.
Blessed is he who, casting aside even for a moment his lack of understanding, plunges into emptiness.

He who, though bound by the snares of treatises composed based on objective entities out of fear, leaps forth with his mind and goes beyond the moat of those very objects— he is a great and solitary deer;
today I have no concern for him, for that single quality of mine which [he once possessed] no longer exists now.
It is specifically for that purpose that I have composed this commentary, which crushes other treatises.
Having studied for a very long time with diligence the *Sūtrasamuccaya*, the *Parikathā*, the *Ratnāvalī*, and the various hymns (*saṃstuti*) spoken in the treatises,
as well as the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā*, the *Ṣaṣṭikā*, the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, and the *Śūnyatāsaptati*;
And that [speech] which was composed for the sake of refuting the argument—that too [he understood]. || 10 ||
Having seen that various kinds of profound sūtras, such as the *Śataka* and others, as well as the commentary composed by Buddhapālita, which is subtle and intended for those of future [capacity],
and whatever has been obtained by me through investigation from the traditional lineage;
Having condensed all this, it has been set forth for the satisfaction of those with lofty intellects. || 11 ||

This Cintāmaṇḍala, the crusher of sophistry, now stands here as the illustrious Candra, illuminating with the rays of his speech the meanings present herein— correctly and without confusion— for those of keen intellect,
while composing this exceedingly clear commentary.
Having risen for the worlds, it destroys their doubts along with the thick darkness. || 12 ||

Having respectfully composed this treatise on the true grammatical system, which provides a clear and unconfused path and relies upon both reasoning and scripture for the sake of establishing certainty among the faithful and the wise—
by whatever vast merit I have gained, as if it were emptiness itself, may the entire world [attain that same state].
Having abandoned the multitude of views, may one proceed upon the path that cuts through all conceptual proliferation.
Having prostrated to the Teacher Gautama, to the perfectly awakened Buddhas who abide in that very nature of reality, to the entire host of the Conqueror’s sons, and to the Dharma spoken by them—
which serves as the eye for embodied beings in perceiving the infinite word of the Buddha— [I shall compose this work].
I bow to that Nāgārjuna who, out of compassion, composed this Madhyamaka.
The *Madhyamakaśāstrastuti* composed by Śrī Candrakīrti is completed.
